content:
Yesterday we looked at Numbers 16 as a whole. Today we begin with the man at the very centre of the rebellion, Korah. His story is especially serious, because Korah was not an outsider attacking Israel. He was a Levite, a Kohathite, already separated for holy service. Yet jealousy and dissatisfaction grew within him until he challenged the order that Yahweh Himself had established.
Some of Israel's greatest dangers arose not from enemies outside, but from inside the camp, through murmuring, unbelief, jealousy, bitterness, and rebellion.

Korah was the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi (Numbers 16:1). This means he belonged to the very family we studied earlier, the Kohathites, and their responsibility was extraordinary. When Israel travelled, the priests first covered the sacred objects, and then the Kohathites carried them upon their shoulders. So, Korah did not have a meaningless position. He belonged to a family entrusted with carrying what was holy through the wilderness.

Yet something changed in his heart. What God had given him began to seem too small. This is revealed by the question Moses put to him, "Is it a small thing to you that the God of Israel has separated you from the congregation of Israel, to bring you near to Himself?" (Numbers 16:9). That question exposes the very beginning of Korah's problem. Korah had been given much, but he was looking at what Aaron had. He was already near, but he wanted to be nearer.He already had a service, but he wanted another man's service. He already had honour, but he wanted another man's position.

Yahweh assigns responsibilities. He had given Israel their camp positions, their marching order, and the Levites their duties. And the lesson for us, the New Creation, is just as clear: we must stop comparing and start obeying, because jealousy over another person's assignment can grow into rebellion against God's own arrangement. So, Moses told Korah plainly, "Are you seeking the priesthood also?" (Numbers 16:10). Here we see the real problem. Korah was not content with the assignment Yahweh had given him. And that dissatisfaction did not remain quietly inside him. Numbers 16:2 tells us that his rebellion eventually included two hundred and fifty leaders of Israel,
well-known and respected men of the congregation. This teaches us something frightening about rebellion: rebellion likes company. Korah could have taken his dissatisfaction before Yahweh. He could have examined himself. He could have gone privately to Moses. Instead, he gathered people around his complaint.

Then together they confronted Moses and Aaron, saying, "You take too much upon yourselves, for all the congregation is holy, every one of them, and Yahweh is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of Yahweh?" (Numbers 16:3). Notice how spiritual their argument sounded. They did not say, "Korah wants Aaron's position." They said, "Everyone is holy." They presented the rebellion as though they were defending the people from proud leaders. And this is one of the great dangers of rebellion: personal ambition can dress itself in spiritual language. Korah could make his own desire sound righteous. He could make Moses and Aaron appear to be the problem. And once enough respected people agreed with him, his complaint could appear justified. But God had appointed Moses. God had appointed Aaron. God had assigned the Kohathites their work. So, Korah was not ultimately fighting Moses and Aaron, and Moses told him so, "Therefore you and all your company are gathered together against Yahweh" (Numbers 16:11). That was the true seriousness of it. Korah thought he was challenging men, but Yahweh said he was challenging Him.

This is perhaps the most frightening part of Korah's story: one person's dissatisfaction did not remain one person's problem. Korah influenced others. Dathan and Abiram joined him. Two hundred and fifty leaders joined him. Eventually much of the congregation was drawn into the controversy. A private dissatisfaction became a public rebellion. Scripture gives us the principle, "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" (1 Corinthians 5:6). When evil rises within the brotherhood and is tolerated, the whole camp can suffer. We must therefore be very careful about whose voices we continually allow into our hearts. Not everyone who agrees with our complaint is helping us. Sometimes we are wrong, and the worst thing we can find is ten friends who tell us we are right. Korah gathered agreement, when what he truly needed was repentance.

We see a strong parallel in Absalom, the son of David, who did something remarkably similar. He stood where people came seeking judgment and told them, "See, your case is good and right; but there is no deputy of the king to hear you" (2 Samuel 15:3). Then he added, "Oh, that I were made judge in the land" (2 Samuel 15:4). Little by little he presented himself as the man who understood the people's problems better than the king, and Scripture says, "So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6). He did not begin by marching an army against David. He first won hearts. He listened to grievances. He created dissatisfaction. He made himself appear sympathetic, and he made the king's government appear inadequate. Then, after winning enough support, the rebellion became open. Korah followed a similar path, gathering influential men, accusing Moses and Aaron, and presenting his challenge as though he were defending the holiness of the congregation.Both rebellions ended in judgment, Korah's when Yahweh Himself showed whom He had appointed, and Absalom's with his death. And so there is a solemn lesson here that we will carry into tomorrow's study: never build a friendship around rebellion. Tomorrow, Yahweh willing, we will see how this same spirit of Korah can appear, much more quietly, within us.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God, who separates and draws near whom You will,
Let us never treat the calling You have given us as though it were a small thing.

Guard us from looking at another's place while despising our own.

Keep us from dressing our own ambition in the language of holiness.

And keep us from gathering others around our complaints when we truly need to repent.

Teach us that to strive against Your order is to strive against You.

"Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for Yahweh." Colossians 3:23

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
